questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The reservoirs and channels at Angkor caught the monsoon and released it slowly across the rice fields through a dry season that lasts half the year. That system, rather than the temples above it, is what allowed a city of several hundred thousand people to stand where no rain falls for six months. Once the channels silted up faster than they could be cleared, the advantage Angkor held over its neighbours _____.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Knot count is the first thing a carpet dealer quotes, and a rug with four hundred knots to the square inch will fetch more than one with a hundred. Weavers themselves treat the number as _____ rather than decisive: fine wool badly dyed, or a design copied by someone who never understood it, makes a poor carpet at any density.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The quilts sewn at Gee's Bend were made from worn work clothes, feed sacks and whatever else a household had to hand. Nothing about the results is _____: blocks are cut off-square on purpose, stripes run out of alignment, and a pattern begun on one edge is abandoned halfway across. Museums that once collected quilts for their neat symmetry now hang these instead.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Horseshoe crab blood clots on contact with traces of bacterial contamination far below what other tests detect, and every injectable drug licensed in the United States is checked with it. Demand has grown until the supply is visibly _____: several hundred thousand animals are bled each year, and counts along parts of the Atlantic coast have fallen for a decade.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “economy” most nearly mean?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Shaker cabinetmakers worked to a rule that whatever was not needed for use should not be made. Drawers go unbanded, chairs are pegged rather than carved, and a whole wall of built-in cupboards may carry no ornament except the run of its own joints. Furniture historians who praise the <u>economy</u> of this work are not talking about what it cost to build.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Anni Albers arrived at the Bauhaus meaning to paint and was directed to the weaving workshop, which was where the women were sent. She stayed. Treating the loom as a set of constraints to work against rather than a craft to be preserved, she wove with cellophane and horsehair, published on the structure of cloth as a subject in its own right, and in 1949 became the first weaver given a solo exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art.

choices.label: A
choices.content: To argue that the Bauhaus was hostile to painting as a discipline.

choices.label: B
choices.content: To describe the technical differences between cellophane and horsehair as fibres.

choices.label: C
choices.content: To catalogue the exhibitions held at the Museum of Modern Art after 1949.

choices.label: D
choices.content: To trace how an assignment she did not choose became the medium of her achievement.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Mary Anning found and prepared the first complete ichthyosaur skeleton to reach London, and dealers and professors bought fossils from her for thirty years. <u>None of the papers those men published on her specimens carried her name.</u> She was never admitted to the Geological Society, which did not accept women, and the labels in the collections holding her work were corrected only long after her death.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It explains the technique she used to prepare the skeleton.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It questions whether the specimens were correctly identified.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It gives the reason the Geological Society was founded.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It introduces the gap between what she contributed and the credit she was given.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Periodical cicadas spend thirteen or seventeen years underground and then emerge in a single week, in numbers no predator can eat through. Both intervals are prime numbers. A predator whose own population peaks every two, three or four years can come into step with a thirteen-year brood only once in a very long while, and the same holds for any hybrid brood emerging on a shorter, non-prime cycle. Broods on even cycles, if they ever existed, would have been eaten out long ago.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Predators of periodical cicadas reach peak numbers every thirteen years.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Hybrid broods survive better than the broods that produced them.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The prime-numbered cycles make it hard for predator populations to fall into step with the cicadas.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Cicadas emerge in a single week because their food is available only then.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Lobstering harbours along the Maine coast are divided into fishing territories that appear on no chart. A boat setting traps on another harbour's ground finds the buoys of its warps cut, and a skipper who persists loses gear faster than he can replace it. The state licenses anyone who qualifies and recognises none of these boundaries. Catches per trap are nonetheless higher inside the tightly held territories than along the stretches of coast where the custom has broken down.

choices.label: A
choices.content: An unofficial system of territories that fishers enforce themselves coincides with better catches.

choices.label: B
choices.content: State licensing has successfully replaced the harbours' informal boundaries.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Cutting another boat's warps is the commonest cause of gear loss in Maine.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Lobster catches are falling everywhere along the Maine coast.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Nyman's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A market town forty minutes from a large city by a rail line opened in 1998 has been surveyed twice, in 1995 and again in 2020. Linguist Peter Nyman argues that the town's distinctive vowel system is being levelled by daily contact with city speech, rather than simply fading of its own accord.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The same vowels have weakened just as much in towns that have no rail link to any city.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Residents surveyed in 2020 said they valued the local accent and hoped it would survive.

choices.label: C
choices.content: In the 2020 survey the older vowels are strongest among residents who never travel to the city and weakest among those who commute there daily.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The town's population grew by roughly a fifth between 1995 and 2020.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Ruiz's claim?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A fresco fragment in a regional museum has been catalogued for a century as the work of an unknown hand. Curator Elena Ruiz argues that it came instead from the workshop of a named master whose documented frescoes survive in two churches within a day's ride of the museum.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Records show that the master received more commissions than his workshop could complete.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The fragment's plaster was laid in daily sections of the same size and order as those in the two documented frescoes, and its underdrawing was transferred from cartoons pricked at the same spacing.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The fragment shows a subject that was painted throughout the region in the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The fragment's plaster was made with sand from a riverbed used by workshops across the whole province.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Halloran's proposal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: An Arctic ground squirrel in hibernation lets its body temperature fall below freezing for weeks at a stretch without ice forming in its tissues. Physiologist Tomas Halloran proposes that the animal manages this by clearing its blood of the particles around which ice crystals would otherwise begin to grow.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Hibernating squirrels rewarm themselves briefly every two or three weeks.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Squirrels hibernate in burrows dug below the depth reached by seasonal frost.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The squirrels' blood contains the same salts, at the same concentrations, as that of related species that do not hibernate.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Blood drawn from hibernating squirrels freezes at a markedly lower temperature than the same blood does after fine particles have been stirred into it.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The tablets from Nineveh were written on unfired clay, which crumbles in damp ground and can be soaked back into mud. When the city was sacked in 612 BCE the palace burned, and the fire was hot enough to bake the tablets stacked in its rooms. Tens of thousands of them were dug out of the ash in the nineteenth century, a great many unbroken and still legible. Paradoxically, then, the destruction of the library _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: left almost nothing for later excavators to recover.

choices.label: B
choices.content: proves the tablets had been fired before they were shelved.

choices.label: C
choices.content: rendered the surviving tablets impossible to read.

choices.label: D
choices.content: is the reason so much of its contents survives.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Some woodland plants attach a small oil-rich body to each seed. Ants carry these seeds back to the nest, feed the oil body to their larvae, and discard the seed itself undamaged in the refuse chamber, a warm pocket of soil enriched by the colony's waste. Plants of this kind advance only a few metres a year. They are scarce in woods that were cleared and replanted within the last century, even where the soil is otherwise suitable, most likely because _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: they have not yet had time to spread into ground that was cleared.

choices.label: B
choices.content: the ants avoid seeds produced by plants growing in young woodland.

choices.label: C
choices.content: such plants require soil that has never been disturbed by ploughing.

choices.label: D
choices.content: the oil bodies grow smaller on plants living in replanted woods.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Rice in the Kerala backwaters grows below sea level, behind earth bunds that have to be pumped dry before every season. Because the fields lie lower than the water on the far side of the _____ a failure of the pumps lasting even a few days will drown a crop that has already been planted.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Meteorites are easier to find on ice than anywhere else, because a dark stone on a white sheet has nowhere to hide. Teams working the blue-ice fields of Antarctica bring back several hundred stones in a _____ most of which have lain where they fell for tens of thousands of years.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Paper was made in China for centuries before the technique travelled west. Craftsmen taken prisoner at Talas in 751 are said to have set up the first mills in _____ within fifty years paper was being made in Baghdad, and within four hundred it had reached Spain.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A roof painted with the new coating stays cooler than the air above it even in full sun. The paint throws back almost all of the sunlight that strikes _____ and it radiates the heat it does absorb at a wavelength that passes straight out through the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The museum's basement holds three hundred safety lamps, each one stamped with the name of the pit that issued it and with the name of the man it was issued to. The _____ names are punched into the brass rather than painted on, which is why they can still be read a century after the last of the pits closed.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Blistering in a glaze is usually a sign that the ware has been brought down through its cooling range too quickly. The kiln was rebuilt over the winter with a taller chimney and a slower cooling cycle. The panels fired in it this spring came out with fewer blisters than _____ fired in the old one.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The panel was painted on oak boards joined edge to edge and held in a frame made for it in the same workshop. Cracks have since opened along one of those joins, and the frame no longer holds the panel square. The conservators recommended that the painting _____ moved until the frame had been rebuilt.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Rammed-earth walls are built from soil compacted inside shuttering, layer by layer, and the soil is normally dug within sight of the wall itself. Walls of this kind need no firing, no cement and almost no transport. _____ they hold heat through the day and give it back after dark, which suits a climate with cold nights.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A written Chinese character gives a reader almost no guide to how the word it stands for is pronounced, which is why speakers of dialects that cannot understand one another in conversation can read the same page. _____ an alphabetic spelling records the sound and leaves the meaning to be worked out from the word itself.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Type was broken up and redistributed as soon as a print run finished, so a book reset for a second printing almost never repeats the errors of the first. Every surviving copy of the 1543 edition carries exactly the same misprint in exactly the same place on page ninety. _____ all of them were pulled from a single setting of the type.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why the drilling stopped short of its target. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Drilling began on the Kola Peninsula in 1970 and was abandoned in 1992.
  • The deepest hole reached 12,262 metres, roughly a third of the way through the crust.
  • Rock at that depth proved much hotter than predicted, about 180 degrees Celsius.
  • The heat made the rock behave plastically, and the hole kept closing on the drill.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Drilling on the Kola Peninsula began in 1970 and was abandoned twenty-two years later.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Rock at 12,262 metres proved far hotter than predicted, about 180 degrees Celsius, and behaved so plastically that the hole kept closing on the drill.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The deepest hole reached about a third of the way through the earth's crust.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The Kola hole is 12,262 metres deep, the deepest ever drilled.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why Johnson's hand calculation was carried out. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Katherine Johnson computed flight trajectories at Langley from 1953.
  • Before the Friendship 7 flight in 1962, NASA had begun calculating orbits on electronic computers.
  • John Glenn would not fly until Johnson had checked the machine's numbers herself.
  • She worked through the same equations on a desk calculator and confirmed the result.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Katherine Johnson had been computing flight trajectories at Langley since 1953.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Because John Glenn would not fly until the electronic computer's figures had been checked by hand, Johnson worked through the same equations herself and confirmed the result.

choices.label: C
choices.content: NASA had begun calculating orbits on electronic computers before the 1962 flight.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Johnson confirmed the orbital figures using a desk calculator.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why returning the oysters is expected to improve the water in the harbour. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • New York Harbor once held roughly 220,000 acres of oyster reef.
  • Dredging, landfill and sewage had destroyed almost all of it by 1920.
  • A single adult oyster filters as much as 190 litres of water a day.
  • Restoration projects have returned more than 100 million oysters to the harbour since 2014.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Restoration projects have returned more than 100 million oysters to New York Harbor since 2014.

choices.label: B
choices.content: New York Harbor once held roughly 220,000 acres of oyster reef, almost all of it destroyed by 1920.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Since a single adult oyster filters as much as 190 litres a day, the more than 100 million oysters returned to the harbour since 2014 are expected to improve its water.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Dredging, landfill and sewage destroyed the harbour's oyster reefs before 1920.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Wang Zhenyi wanted to explain a lunar eclipse to readers who had none of the mathematics. She set a lamp on a table for the sun, hung a round mirror above it for the moon, and moved a garden globe between them for the earth until its shadow fell exactly where she wanted it. The demonstration was _____: anyone standing in the room could see for herself why the moon went dark.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A naked mole-rat colony contains one breeding female, and the hundred or so animals around her do not reproduce at all. They dig, carry food and defend the tunnels on behalf of a queen whose young are their siblings rather than their offspring. Among mammals the arrangement is nearly _____: outside a couple of African burrowers it is found only in insects.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “qualify” most nearly mean?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A Noh mask is carved to hold one expression and no more. The actor cannot alter it, but he can turn it: tipped a few degrees toward the light the mask reads as grief, and tipped back it reads as composure. Nothing on the wood has moved. Critics who write that the angle of the head can <u>qualify</u> the mask mean that the carving by itself never settles what an audience sees.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Cross-laminated timber is made by gluing boards in layers, with the grain of each layer turned across the grain of the one below it. Wood is strong along the grain and weak across it, so alternating the direction produces a panel that behaves much the same way in both directions and can carry a floor load. The strength of the panel is thus a product of its _____ rather than of the species of tree it came from.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Delia Derbyshire had no synthesiser when she realised the theme in 1963. Every note in it is a length of magnetic tape cut from a recording of a plucked wire or a filtered oscillator, trimmed until it sounded the right pitch, and spliced to the note after it. Assembling a single minute took days of measuring and cutting. The finished piece sounds effortless, which _____ the labour behind it.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The detector's two arms are four kilometres long, and a passing gravitational wave stretches one and squeezes the other by less than the width of a proton. <u>A lorry on a road twenty kilometres away shifts the mirrors far more than the signal does.</u> Each site therefore records hundreds of channels of local vibration alongside the main measurement, and a candidate event is kept only if it appears at both sites, thousands of kilometres apart, within the time light needs to travel between them.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It compares two methods of measuring the length of the arms.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It explains how gravitational waves are produced.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It states the problem that the arrangement described afterwards is built to solve.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It concedes that the detector has never recorded a genuine signal.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Once a year the Athenian assembly voted on whether an ostracism should be held at all. If it voted yes, citizens gathered two months later and scratched a name on a broken potsherd. <u>The man named on the most sherds left Attica for ten years, keeping his property and his citizenship.</u> Thousands of sherds have since been dug out of the city's wells, and several bundles carry the same name in the same handwriting, which suggests that some were prepared in advance for voters to collect.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It specifies what the vote actually did to the man it named.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It explains why the sherds ended up in the city's wells.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It offers evidence that the outcome of the vote was manipulated.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It defines the general powers of the Athenian assembly.

questions.stem: Based on the text, what does the pottery sequence indicate?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The stone walls at Great Zimbabwe stand up to eleven metres high and were laid without mortar, each granite block cut to sit on the one beneath it. European visitors in the nineteenth century credited them to Phoenicians, Arabs, anyone but the people living around them. Excavation has since produced Chinese celadon, Persian glass and a great deal of local pottery, and the pottery below the walls is continuous with the pottery above them.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The walls were built by traders who had arrived from Persia.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The site was abandoned before the walls were finished.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Chinese celadon reached the site before the earliest walls were raised.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The community already living on the site was the one that built the walls.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A Japanese woodblock print is signed by the artist who drew it, and the drawing itself is destroyed in the making. The block cutter pastes it face down on cherry wood and cuts away everything the artist did not draw, so the lines survive only as the ridges left standing. Printers then pull one impression for every colour, holding the sheet in place with two notches cut into each block. Publishers, who paid for all of it, chose the subjects.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The registration notches were the printers' most important invention.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Publishers seldom influenced the subjects of the prints they financed.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A print credited to one artist is in fact the product of several trades.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Block cutters were more highly skilled than the artists who signed the prints.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Tesfaye's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A stand of bamboo may flower once in a century, and when it does every plant in the stand flowers at the same time, sets seed and dies. Biologist Rahel Tesfaye argues that the long interval and the synchrony are both defences: seed-eating animals cannot maintain a population on a food supply that appears twice in a lifetime, and the quantity released at once exceeds anything the animals present can eat.

choices.label: A
choices.content: In a mass-flowering year rodent numbers climb sharply, yet the proportion of seed eaten is far lower than in stands that flower in small patches every year.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Bamboo stands that flower synchronously grow at higher altitudes than stands that do not.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Bamboo seedlings grow more quickly in shade than in full sun.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Rodents in bamboo forests eat fruit and insects when no seed is available.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Braga's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A Roman fort on the northern frontier has produced cooking pots of a shape not made anywhere in the surrounding province. Archaeologist Sonia Braga argues that the unit garrisoned there was raised on the Rhine and brought its own foodways north with it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Pots of the same shape have been found at forts across the empire, including in North Africa.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A dedication stone from the fort names an emperor who reigned for two years.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Chemical analysis shows the pots were made from clay dug within a few kilometres of the fort, in shapes otherwise recorded only in the Rhineland.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The pots are the commonest single find in the fort's rubbish pits.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Molina's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Female vampire bats that fail to find a meal are fed by roostmates, which regurgitate part of what they took. Behavioural ecologist Ines Molina argues that the sharing is sustained by reciprocity between particular individuals rather than by kinship alone.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Among unrelated bats housed together, how readily one bat donates to a given partner tracks how often that partner has fed it in the past.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Bats that share blood tend to roost closer together than bats that do not.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Mothers donate to their own pups far more often than to any other bat in the roost.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A vampire bat can survive only about sixty hours without a blood meal.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Lithium is expensive and unevenly distributed. Sodium sits directly below it in the periodic table, behaves similarly, and is abundant almost everywhere. Sodium-ion cells work on the same principle as lithium-ion ones, but a sodium ion is larger and heavier, so a cell of a given mass stores less energy. Sodium cells also tolerate being run flat and cost less per kilowatt-hour. It follows that sodium-ion cells are best suited to uses in which _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: the cell must never be allowed to discharge fully.

choices.label: B
choices.content: lithium happens to be locally abundant.

choices.label: C
choices.content: the weight of the battery matters less than what it costs.

choices.label: D
choices.content: the battery must be made as light as it possibly can be.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A clock runs more slowly the deeper it sits in a gravitational field, an effect so small that only atomic timekeeping can register it over short distances. Two identical optical clocks were compared, one left on a laboratory bench and the other raised thirty centimetres above it on a support. Over several days the raised clock ran measurably ahead of the one below. If the same comparison were repeated with the upper clock raised a full metre instead, the gap that opened between the two clocks would _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: grow larger than it did at thirty centimetres.

choices.label: B
choices.content: reverse, so that the lower clock ran ahead.

choices.label: C
choices.content: stay exactly what it was at thirty centimetres.

questions.passage: Optics before him rested on the idea that the eye sends something out towards whatever it sees. Ibn al-Haytham, the scholar who wrote the Book of Optics while under house arrest in _____ instead that light travels from the object to the eye, and tested the claim with a darkened room and a pinhole.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The Hanseatic ships that worked the Baltic sailed on a short list of goods. The league's warehouse at Bergen dealt in almost nothing _____ dried cod from the north, grain out of the eastern ports and salt carried up from the Bay of Biscay.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The abbey stands on a rock in a bay with one of the largest tidal ranges in Europe. When the tide runs out across the _____ the causeway is dry for six hours and the island stops being an island at all.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A portolan chart is drawn from sailing directions rather than from any survey. Although nobody who made these charts had a means of fixing longitude at _____ the outlines of the Mediterranean on the earliest of them are accurate to within a few kilometres.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The studio's negatives came to the archive in tea chests, unlabelled and in no order, and nobody has been able to say how many of them there are. A grant from the trust now covers the whole of the work. It pays for cataloguing the negatives, digitising the most fragile among them, and _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: to make the entire collection searchable online.

choices.label: B
choices.content: for the searching of the entire collection online.

choices.label: C
choices.content: making the entire collection searchable online.

questions.stem: A kayak outfitter's total charge, in dollars, for a rental lasting h hours is given by \(C=18+7h\). What is the total charge, in dollars, for a rental lasting 4 hours?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A snow plough clears a mountain road, and \(L(t)=45-9t\) gives the number of kilometres of that road still uncleared t hours after the plough sets out. How many kilometres are still uncleared 3 hours after the plough sets out?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A safety notice at a via ferrata bridge states that the number of climbers n on the bridge must be fewer than 9 at any moment. Which inequality gives all the possible values of n?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A ropemaker's twisting frame produces \(P(h)=24h\) metres of rope after running for h hours. For how many hours must the frame run to produce 180 metres of rope?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A stagehand counts the lamps on a lighting bar as \(4(3n-7)+5n\), where n is the number of sections in the bar. Which expression is equivalent to the number of lamps?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A greengrocer packs \(x^{4}\) plums into each layer of a crate and puts \(x^{2}\) layers in the crate, where \(x>1\). Which expression gives the number of plums in the crate?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A lens grinder finds that polishing a mirror of diameter d centimetres takes \(T(d)=d^{2}+5\) minutes. How many minutes does polishing a mirror of diameter 7 centimetres take?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A mat of duckweed doubles in area every week, and \(A(w)=3(2)^{w}\) gives its area in square metres w weeks after it is first measured. What is the area of the mat, in square metres, 4 weeks after it is first measured?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A puzzle-box maker sets p pegs into each face of a box, and her design rule requires \(p^{2}-9=40\), where p is positive. How many pegs are set into each face?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A mosaicist lays a rectangular panel that is \((x+4)\) tiles long and \((x-9)\) tiles wide. Which expression gives the number of tiles in the panel?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A dyer's recipe uses 5 grams of madder root for every 2 litres of water. At that rate, how many grams of madder root are needed for 14 litres of water?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: Of the 420 paper lanterns hung along a canal for a festival, 35% are red. How many of those lanterns are red?
questions.subject: MATH

Sea stackNesting pairs
Craigan128

Altogether, how many nesting pairs were recorded on the three sea stacks that season?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The numbers of eggs counted in six wrens' nests are 4, 5, 5, 6, 7 and 9. What is the mean number of eggs per nest?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The gable end of a garden shed is a right triangle, and one of its acute angles measures 37° . What is the measure, in degrees, of the other acute angle?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The floor of a hexagonal gazebo is laid as 6 identical triangular sections, and each section covers 2.5 square metres. What is the total area of the gazebo floor, in square metres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A circular lily pond has a radius of 6 metres. The area of the pond, in square metres, can be written as \(k\pi\). What is the value of k?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A chandler pours 4.5 litres of melted wax equally into 6 moulds. How many litres of wax go into each mould?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A model rocket's altitude, in metres, is given by \(a(t)=5t^{2}\), where t is the number of seconds since it was launched. What is the rocket's altitude, in metres, 6 seconds after it is launched?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A rigger's turnbuckle sits at the right-angled corner \(E\) of a triangular stay \(DEF\), whose leg \(DE\) measures 8 metres and whose leg \(EF\) measures 15 metres. What is the value of \(\tan D\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A cartographer draws two straight contour lines in the xy-plane. One is the graph of \(y=\frac{3}{5}x-4\) and the other is the graph of \(3x-my=25\), where m is a constant. The two contour lines never meet. What is the value of m?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A cable railway charges \(F(d)=a+bd\) francs for a journey of d kilometres, where a and b are constants. A 6-kilometre journey costs 27 francs and a 14-kilometre journey costs 51 francs. What is the value of \(a+b\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A tour operator's minibus has 17 seats and runs only when every seat is filled. An adult seat costs $32 and a child seat costs $19, and the operator must take at least $460 from the journey. What is the greatest number of children who can travel on that journey?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: Two sluice gates opened together drain a mill pond in 6 hours. The larger gate on its own would drain the pond in 5 hours less than the smaller gate on its own would. How many hours would the smaller gate on its own take to drain the pond?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A dye works puts every skein through two treatments modelled by \(p(x)=2x-5\) and \(q(x)=x^{2}+1\), applied in that order so that the value p produces is fed into q. Which expression is equivalent to \(q(p(x))\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A wind-tunnel scaling law is quoted as \(\left(\frac{16x^{8}}{y^{-4}}\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}\), where \(x>0\) and \(y>0\), and an engineer must rewrite it so that no exponent is a fraction. Which expression is equivalent to that scaling law?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A bridge designer models the underside of an arch by \(f(x)=2x^{2}+bx+18\), where b is a positive constant. The graph of \(y=f(x)\) meets the x-axis at exactly one point. What is the value of b?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A brewer's blending ratio for a cask is \(\frac{x^{2}-9}{x^{2}+x-12}\), where \(x>4\). Which expression is equivalent to that blending ratio?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The cross-section of a skate ramp is modelled by \(y=a(x-4)^{2}-12\), where a is a positive constant, and the modelled curve passes through the point \((10,15)\). What is the value of a?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: In the xy-plane, the parabola \(y=x^{2}-4x+7\) and the line \(y=2x+c\), where c is a constant, cross at exactly two points. Which of the following could be the value of c?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A chemist records the contents of a reaction vessel twice, as \(4x-3y=7\) and as \(8x+ay=1\), where a is a constant. For exactly one value of a there is no pair \((x,y)\) satisfying both records. What is that value of a?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A researcher recruited 300 volunteers and randomly assigned each of them either to a new stretching routine or to their usual routine. After twelve weeks the volunteers on the new routine had significantly greater gains in flexibility than the others. Which conclusion is best supported by this study?
questions.subject: MATH

choices.label: A
choices.content: Flexibility gains and stretching routines are unrelated among the volunteers in the study.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Volunteers who take up stretching routines on their own are more flexible than volunteers who do not.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The new stretching routine will produce greater gains in flexibility for every adult in the country.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The new stretching routine caused greater gains in flexibility for the volunteers in the study.

questions.stem: A vineyard measures the sugar content of eleven grape samples and records, in degrees Brix, the values 19, 20, 20, 21, 21, 22, 22, 22, 23, 24 and 41. Which statement about these eleven values is true?
questions.subject: MATH

choices.label: A
choices.content: The mean is less than the median.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The mean is equal to the median.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The mean is greater than the median.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The mean is greater than every one of the recorded values.

questions.stem: A tannery mixes a brine that is 12% salt by mass with a brine that is 30% salt by mass to obtain 45 litres of brine that is 18% salt by mass. How many litres of the 30% brine does the tannery use?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A surveyor sights across a river and obtains two similar triangles \(PQR\) and \(PST\), where S lies on \(\overline{PQ}\), T lies on \(\overline{PR}\) and \(\overline{ST}\) is parallel to \(\overline{QR}\). The measurements are \(PS=12\) metres, \(SQ=18\) metres and \(QR=45\) metres. What is the length of \(\overline{ST}\), in metres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A solid brass sphere of radius 6 centimetres is melted down and cast, with no loss of brass, into solid cylindrical rods of radius 2 centimetres and length 9 centimetres. How many complete rods can be cast from the sphere?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A ship's radar plot forms a right triangle \(XYZ\) with the right angle at \(Y\). The leg \(XY\) measures 9 nautical miles and the leg \(YZ\) measures 40 nautical miles. What is the value of \(\cos X\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A community kitchen will cook exactly 20 kilograms of pulses, made up of lentils and beans. Each kilogram of lentils yields 6 portions and each kilogram of beans yields 4 portions, and the kitchen must serve at least 90 portions. What is the least number of kilograms of lentils the kitchen can use?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: In a three-stage relay the first runner's leg is 3 times as long as the second runner's leg, and the third runner's leg is 400 metres shorter than the first runner's leg. The three legs together measure 3,800 metres. How many metres long is the second runner's leg?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A sailmaker's cutting line on a plan passes through the points \((-2,9)\) and \((6,-7)\) in the xy-plane. What is the x-coordinate of the point where this cutting line crosses the x-axis?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A water trough is a prism 2 metres long whose cross-section is a trapezium with parallel sides of 40 centimetres and 60 centimetres and a perpendicular height of 30 centimetres. Given that 1 litre is 1,000 cubic centimetres, how many litres of water does the full trough hold?
questions.subject: MATH
